body_markdown:
“They just don’t get it.”


That’s the sentiment I often hear from my fellow graybeards on the subject of young people and their interest—or lack thereof—in cars. “They only care about their phones and video games,” is another common lament.


As we have been reporting for years, it’s[hogwash](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/hagerty-magazine/car-enthusiasm-is-safe-with-the-next-generation/) .


I understand the genuine anxiety about a generation that seems more comfortable with a screen than a steering wheel. As I’ve said repeatedly in this space,[the research](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) on the benefits of physical engagement, hands-on problem solving, and real-world community is not nothing. Cars happen to be one of the great gateways into all three.


But I suspect a lot of the grumbling I hear in person and read online has less to do with the youthful members of the Gen Z and Millennial generations and more to do with the value of the aging grumblers’ car collections.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


To the grumblers, I say, *chill, dudes.* And I also say, I wish you could have been with me the weekend before last in Monterey, California, where I attended[Gridlife](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/gridlife-the-answer-to-the-rulebook-blues/) at WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca. I’d heard about this event, a mashup between track day and music festival, but didn’t know what to expect. I did expect young people, of course, and I wasn’t onsite long before I realized that I was one of the oldest people there. Which I loved.


Before I get into my Gridlife experience, some history: The event was co-founded by Chris Stewart and Adam Jabaay,[who met at a Jimmy Eat World concert](https://autos.yahoo.com/people-and-culture/articles/gridlifes-co-founder-talks-going-185000943.html) when Stewart left a note on Jabaay’s Honda hatchback in the parking lot. Stewart had been hosting Honda meets and track days at GingerMan Raceway in west Michigan since 2004. The first official Gridlife, in May 2014, offered a simple but very innovative formula: racing during the day—time attack, drifting, high-performance driving events, and wheel-to-wheel competition—and live music concerts after the track went cold at night.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


For Stewart, a former advertising creative director, Gridlife was simply taking all his individual passions and mashing them together. His mission statement was simple: *motorsports inclusion.* Lower every barrier—cost, intimidation, snobbery—and put as many kinds of car people as possible in the same place at the same time.[The 2014 debut drew over 1500 spectators.](https://grassrootsmotorsports.com/articles/gridlife-founding-series/) A decade later the Midwest Festival alone draws 22,000 people over a weekend. Earlier this year Stewart and Jabaay[sold the business](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/gridlife-has-new-owners-will-its-events-have-the-same-vibe/) to a new ownership group to help scale it further, and both stayed in leadership roles.


The paddock at Laguna Seca was full of all kinds of folks in their teens, 20s, and 30s—spectating, racing, wrenching, and fully invested. A Monterey local told me that he thought there were more folks at Gridlife than at the recent IMSA sports car race. And it wasn’t just dudes, a stark contrast to the club racing I’ve done for decades. As the old guy (I’m 56), walking around, I asked a bunch of people why they were there and what they liked.


Two things I heard repeatedly: They loved “the vibe” and, perhaps more surprisingly, the culture. Culture, I probed? The answer came back different ways from different people but the message was consistent—they appreciated how the car community came together at Gridlife, how it felt less like a commercial event and more like a gathering of people who genuinely had each other’s backs. Sure, there was a competitive element to some of the racing, but I saw little of the testosterone-fueled chest-beating I’m more familiar with at my racing venues.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Here’s a perfect example of that vibe: During a press conference on Friday, musician and drifter T-Pain[presented a gift](https://www.rtrvehicles.com/blogs/news/t-pain-gifts-hert-a-910-hp-mustang-rtr-drift-car-introducing-the-twerk-horse?srsltid=AU7gw4VoErsy2mwdFyHSURaTaZukjiljt3ZeMo4uml8al0D16LnYFZpQ) —a drift car—to fellow competitor Hertrech Eugene Jr., known universally as Hert, whose previous car had been destroyed in a crash. The crowd went wild.


Capturing content is also part of the draw.[Hagerty video host Larry Chen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/series/capturing-car-culture/) , a major celebrity at Gridlife, films the drifters up close with a[camera mounted on the nose](https://youtu.be/2n4AKEPW2Ow?si=rSRw5ej9jbZVkMuy) of a Toyota Supra. During one of the drift sessions, as I rode shotgun, Chen maneuvered, at triple-digit speeds, mere inches from the sliding cars that were often obscured by heavy tire smoke. When we slowed, I heard the spectators—yes, there was a crowd for this—cheering *Lar-ree, Lar-ree, Lar-ree.* I knew that was not for me, lol. Everyone had their phones out.


On Saturday night, the track was transformed into a concert venue with bars and a stage. People danced to a DJ named[Kaivon](https://kaivonmusic.com/) . One guy danced while holding a tire over his head. In a nearby tent furnished with couches and gaming consoles, people played Microsoft’s *Forza* driving game *.* In fact, some attendees told me that Gridlife is the IRL (In Real Life) version of *Forza* . A nearby paddock area was filled with tents. I saw plenty of JDM (Japanese Domestic Market) and post-1980s German cars, with some American iron sprinkled in. I didn’t see any exotics like Ferraris or McLarens.


> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdwmjZ8mtvl/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
>
> [A post shared by Gridlife Laguna (@gridlifelaguna)](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdwmjZ8mtvl/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


As for the racing, I was all in, renting a relatively new type of racing car called the Rush SR. The company was started in 2017 by father and son[David and Blair Hosie](https://rushautoworks.com/about/) to build an inexpensive yet fast race car. The Rush is a single-seat, steel-framed pocket rocket powered by a Suzuki motorcycle engine. New, the cars cost about $50,000, and they’re the hottest thing in amateur road racing: The company has sold about 400 cars that are built in a Houston factory.


The California Rush dealer charged me $6000 for the weekend, and the entry fee was $1500. For that I got four 12-lap races, two practices, and one qualifying session. By the standards of Laguna track time, that was cheap, a fact that did not escape others: There were some 50 other Rushes in my race, all mandated to have the same equipment as mine.


> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdrxvkxSbuy/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
>
> [A post shared by Bobby Yu (@bobbyuvisuals)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdrxvkxSbuy/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


Consequently, the racing was a madhouse, a swarm of bees circling the track. About half the racing laps were spent under full course yellow warning flags, because crashes were common. I got the sense that my team wasn’t set up for major weekend repairs, so I knew any crash would likely end my weekend. Caution, however, was folly. I caught some drivers who were exhibiting questionable driving, so I knew a big mistake would soon make for an easy and safe pass. But any hesitation meant four cars would pass *me* . I figured that any start gave me a fifty-fifty chance of getting taken out as the swarm converged on Laguna’s Turn 2. I love driving that track and didn’t want to miss a lap.


The Rush is wickedly fast, much quicker than what I usually race. One driver said he liked the machine because there was so much to learn and perfect. That sounds about right. I steadily improved over the weekend and finished 28th in the final race. Humbling. The leaders put on quite a show; watch it[here.](https://youtu.be/S9zevkjRF_U?si=Rw1Q103PL-5U0ssz)


I came home with something I did not need but was glad to have confirmed—the kids are absolutely alright.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


They always were. Anyone who has spent time around young people and cars already knows this. Those who fret about the next generation are not really worried about whether young people love cars; they are worried that the love looks different from their own. It does. The wrapper has changed. The music is louder, the cars are different, and someone is dancing with a tire over his head. But the impulse—to find your people, to drive something exciting, to be part of something—is identical to what pulled every one of us in.


The Gridlife crowd also was genuinely welcoming to a senior guy wandering around asking questions. Nobody made me feel out of place. A few even seemed curious about what I was doing there—which is exactly how I felt about them, and exactly how this is supposed to work.


I think we should all embrace it. Go to a Gridlife event (this year had six of them, spread across the USA). Ask people why they are there and watch them have their own kind of automotive fun. You will come home, as I did, a little humbled but a lot more optimistic. The hobby is in good hands. They just hold their phones a little differently than we did.


Never Stop Driving


Larry
